title: Influencing factors of urban drone delivery choice behavior in the context of the low-altitude economy; [低空经济下城市无人机配送选择行为影响因素研究]
author: Wang, Liao and Jingrou, Deng and Tao, Li
journal: Journal of Shenzhen University Science and Engineering
abstract: Driven by the development of the low-altitude economy, drone delivery has emerged as a new driver for upgrading urban logistics systems. To investigate urban residents' preferences and decision-making mechanisms regarding drone delivery services, this study takes Shenzhen, China, as a case study. Based on random utility theory, revealed preferences (RP) and stated preferences (SP) surveys are conducted, and discrete choice models are employed to examine the effects of key factors on residents' actual choice behavior towards drone delivery services and the associated value conversion. The results show that residents exhibit risk-averse decision-making characteristics, and factors including safety, delivery cost, delivery time, and noise significantly influence the acceptance of drone delivery. Although variables such as gender, residential floor level, and residential location do not show significant main effects, their interaction effects with delivery cost and safety are significant, indicating that individual characteristics affect acceptance through interaction mechanisms. The effects of different factors vary substantially: safety and delivery cost have the greatest impacts on residents' choice behavior, followed by delivery time, while noise has the weakest effect. Furthermore, residents demonstrate different levels of sensitivity to these factors, with scenarios characterized by high safety and low delivery fees being the most attractive. Therefore, improving delivery safety and controlling delivery costs are essential for enhancing public acceptance of drone delivery, while differentiated strategies should be developed according to the distinct characteristics of different population groups. © 2026 Science Press. title: Validation and application of the Chinese version of the abbreviated math anxiety scale
author: Peng, Yafeng and Zeng, Jinxin and Chen, Hui and Li, Yujun
abstract: Background: Evidence on the psychometric performance of the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (AMAS) and the heterogeneity of math anxiety among Chinese secondary-school students remains limited. This study evaluated the Chinese version of the AMAS (AMAS-C) and examined latent profiles of math anxiety and their associations with demographic and educational variables. Methods: Participants were 936 secondary-school students from Guangdong and Jiangxi, China. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega. Confirmatory factor analysis, external construct-validity analysis, and item response theory were used to evaluate the scale's measurement properties. Latent profile analysis was conducted on the nine AMAS items, followed by proportional-odds logistic regression. Results: The AMAS-C showed good internal consistency (α = 0.87; ω = 0.89), and its total score was negatively associated with mathematics attitudes (r = −0.57). The bifactor model provided the best fit in both the CFA and IRT comparisons. This model included a dominant general math-anxiety factor and two orthogonal context-specific factors representing residual variation associated with learning and evaluation situations. The test information function showed that the AMAS-C provided adequate measurement precision across a broad range of math-anxiety levels. LPA identified three quantitatively ordered profiles—Low Anxiety Across Both Contexts (24.6%), Intermediate Anxiety with Pronounced Evaluation Anxiety (50.0%), and High Anxiety Across Both Contexts (25.4%). These profiles differed in overall anxiety level and the relative prominence of learning and evaluation anxiety. Gender and mathematics performance were significantly associated with profile membership, whereas school stage, only-child status, and region were not. Female students had higher cumulative odds of belonging to a higher-anxiety profile than male students (OR = 1.70, 95% CI [1.32, 2.19]). Poorer mathematics performance was associated with lower predicted probabilities of first-profile membership and higher probabilities of third-profile membership. The predicted probability of second-profile membership peaked in intermediate performance categories. Conclusions: The AMAS-C demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity evidence among Chinese secondary-school students. Among the candidate models examined, the bifactor model provided a reasonable working representation of the data, with a predominant general math anxiety factor. The IRT results indicated adequate item functioning and useful measurement precision across a range of math anxiety levels. The LPA identified three ordered profiles: Low Anxiety Across Both Contexts, Intermediate Anxiety with Pronounced Evaluation Anxiety, and High Anxiety Across Both Contexts. These profiles differed in overall anxiety level and the relative prominence of learning- and evaluation-related anxiety. Female students and students reporting poorer mathematics performance were more likely to belong to higher-anxiety profiles, whereas school stage, only-child status, and region showed no statistically significant independent associations with profile membership. © 2026 The Authors. title: Leaving on a High or Low Note? An Achievement Goal Perspective on Executive Retirement
author: Huang, Zhefan and Wang, Kaidi and Lu, Bingjie and Wang, Mo and Hill, Aaron D. and Pryor, Christopher
abstract: Executive retirement represents a pivotal career transition with significant implications. However, our understanding of the antecedents of executive retirement remains limited. We contend that, different from the retirement of general employees, it is important to position executive retirement within an achievement context and consider factors such as firm performance and achievement goal orientations. Drawing on late adulthood developmental psychology, we propose an achievement goal framework to theorize the relationship between firm performance and executive retirement, and the moderating roles of goal orientations. We theorize that firm performance is associated with two distinct mechanisms: the legacy fulfillment mechanism (salient for executives with high performance) and the selective prioritization mechanism (salient for executives with low performance), which together result in a U-shaped relationship between firm performance and the likelihood of executive retirement. We further consider executives’ goal orientations as boundary conditions to probe the underlying mechanisms. We found general support for our theory using an archival dataset of 1840 chief executive officers from S&P 1500 firms (Study 1) and a two-wave survey of 363 executives (Study 2). By integrating developmental psychology theories into the executive retirement literature, our research sheds light on executive retirement decisions through a developmental psychology lens. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era
author: Fortuna, Paweł
journal: Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era
abstract: Well-being supported by digital technologies, grounded in research-based frameworks Researchers and practitioners need systematic approaches to studying how technology enhances rather than diminishes human flourishing. Positive Cyberpsychology: Human Flourishing in a Digital Era introduces PCyb as a field examining factors and processes that support well-being in digital interactions. Paweł Fortuna, one of the pioneers in positive cyberpsychology with over 50 peer-reviewed publications, provides the first comprehensive English-language framework for this emerging field. The book integrates and systematizes empirical findings using the psychological models of flourishing across health, relationships, personal growth, education and work contexts. Structured around three guiding questions—Why is PCyb? What is PCyb? How is PCyb?—it traces the field’s disciplinary development, connects positive psychology with cyberpsychology into a coherent integrative framework. Theoretical insights are combined with empirically grounded examples for immediate research application. Readers will also find: A concrete research framework that outlines specific psychological investigations rather than general approaches to technology design In-depth analysis revealing strong connections between positive psychology, cyberpsychology, and design practices for well-being-oriented digital experiences Concepts, directions, and methods for studying digital strengths, digital well-being, positive technology interventions, and the upward dynamics of flourishing in digital contexts. Evidence-informed insights relevant to implementing flourishing-oriented solutions across diverse contexts spanning AI-driven systems, applications, social media platforms, immersive technologies and gaming. Theoretical foundations combined with actionable examples suitable for coursework in cyberpsychology, positive psychology, AI ethics, and design Researchers and students in psychology, cyberpsychology, AI, and digital humanities will find essential and integrative frameworks and a rich source of research directions for advancing well-being-focused technology studies. Technology designers, UX specialists, and educators developing courses in positive psychology or ethical AI will gain research-informed guidance for shaping digital experiences that genuinely support human flourishing. © 2027 by John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

title: Putting assumptions to the test: A meta-analytic review of gender differences in emotional intelligence and specific emotion abilities.
author: Hausfeld, Mary M. and Hampel, Vera and Bach, Leon J. and Menges, Jochen I.
abstract: Are women more emotionally intelligent than men? Emotional intelligence (EI) is often colloquially ascribed to women, yet the extant empirical literature yields inconclusive results and EI theories are largely oblivious to gender as an explanatory dimension. To re-evaluate the literature, test key moderators, and develop stronger theory on EI, we examine whether and to what extent gender differences manifest in EI through a meta-analytic review of 1,279 articles comprised of 1,428 samples containing 609,278 participants drawn from published and unpublished work until December 31, 2023. The results suggest gender differences in general EI such that women appear to have higher EI on average, as well as more nuanced gender differences across specific emotional abilities, including some where there may be no difference. Women's advantage is stronger for other- than self-focused emotional abilities and varies by measurement type, with smaller differences in subjective than in performance-based assessments. Additionally, we find that contextual moderators, including leadership position, male-dominated industry, data collection year, participant age, and geographical region, are associated with the presence, magnitude, and direction of gender differences, suggesting that gender differences in EI vary across contexts. Overall, these findings show that women hold advantages in many emotional abilities, but that gender differences in EI are contingent on the target of emotional abilities, measurement type, and context, informing future research and theory building. title: Unemployment in later life: The effects of a job search skills training intervention and development orientations on job search and reemployment of older job seekers.
author: van den Hee, Sarah M. and van Hooft, Edwin A. J. and Van Hoye, Greet and Nevicka, Barbara
abstract: Late-career unemployment has a demonstrated negative impact on individuals and society. Yet little is known about the mechanisms through which policy programs operate to support older unemployed individuals in finding reemployment. The present study aimed to provide more insight into how a job search skills training program facilitates older job seekers in their reemployment process and who benefits most from the program. Using a two-group field experimental design among 4,625 unemployed job seekers aged over 50, we examined the effects of the job search skills training intervention on participants’ job search knowledge and self-efficacy, job search behaviors, and reemployment status and speed. In addition, the study examined whether the effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy depend on older job seekers’ development orientations (i.e., future time perspective and learning goal orientation). Job search skills training was found to increase older job seekers’ job search knowledge and self-efficacy, and in turn their job search process quality, which then enhanced their chances and speed of finding reemployment. The positive effects of job search skills training on job search knowledge and self-efficacy appeared to be stronger for older job seekers with lower development orientations. The current findings advance training and job search theory by uncovering the explanatory mechanisms of a job search skills training program and by showing that individual attributes influence learning outcomes. Our findings also have important implications for the design, implementation, and evaluation of future policy programs aimed at older unemployed individuals and career counseling practice. title: A meta-analytic examination of the criterion-related validity and cognitive loading associated with traditional and new situational judgment test paradigms.
author: Lievens, Filip and Zhou, You and Ng, Jomel Wei Xuan and Xi, Liyan and Tian, Yixin and Sackett, Paul R. and Martin-Raugh, Michelle
abstract: Traditionally, situational judgment tests (SJTs) include text-based situations and ask candidates to pick the best and worst response option. Over the years, various new SJT paradigms have been developed to increase validity, reduce incidental cognitive load, and/or lower costs. Examples are multimedia SJTs, constructed response SJTs, and single-response SJTs. First, this study investigates how the traditional SJT paradigm performs in terms of criterion-related validity by updating prior meta-analyses. Second, this study provides initial, meta-analytic evidence on the criterion-related validity and cognitive load of several new SJT paradigms. On the basis of 457 independent samples from 302 studies (total N = 244,257), results showed that SJTs were not only predictive of job performance but also of academic performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and counterproductive work behavior. SJT validity was higher in operational (i.e., applicant) settings than in nonoperational settings and could also be expanded to new content (e.g., emotion and cross-cultural management). In terms of comparing traditional and new SJT paradigms, multimedia SJTs had validity equal to text-based ones but lower cognitive load. Importantly, the multiple-choice modality did not significantly outperform written constructed response modalities in terms of validity, and the cognitive loading of webcam-constructed responses was even lower than that of other response modalities. The implications of these findings are among others discussed in the context of the cost effectiveness of SJTs vis-à-vis other selection procedures. title: Acculturative stress and internalizing problems among Latinos who drink hazardously: The roles of distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation.
author: Mallin, Emily L. and Silva, Karina and Amarneh, Dania Y. and Cotton, Mallory R. and Hernandez Ortiz, Jessica and Trent, Erika S. and Zvolensky, Michael J. and Viana, Andres G.
abstract: Although acculturative stress contributes significantly to internalizing problems among Latinos who drink hazardously, the individual difference variables that strengthen or weaken this relationship have remained elusive. To address this gap, we examined two cognitive–affective factors, namely, distress tolerance and emotion dysregulation, as candidate moderators. We expected that acculturative stress would be positively associated with internalizing problems (operationalized as anxious arousal, traumatic intrusions, and social anxiety) at lower levels of distress tolerance and/or higher levels of emotion dysregulation. A sample of Latinos who drink hazardously (N = 99) completed measures of acculturative stress, distress tolerance, emotion dysregulation, and internalizing symptoms. There was a significant Acculturative Stress × Distress Tolerance interaction explaining 5.02% and 4.19% of the variance in anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions, respectively. Acculturative stress was significantly positively associated with anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions only at lower levels of distress tolerance. There was also a significant Acculturative Stress × Emotion Dysregulation interaction explaining 7.46% of the variance in anxious arousal. Acculturative stress was significantly positively associated with anxious arousal only at higher levels of emotion dysregulation. Acculturative stress was associated with anxious arousal and traumatic intrusions among Latinos who drink hazardously with lower distress tolerance and/or higher emotion dysregulation. Enhancing distress tolerance and lowering emotion dysregulation may protect Latino individuals who engage in hazardous drinking and experience acculturative stress against internalizing problems, and these processes may serve as targets in future intervention programming.
